extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history and criticism; artists, sculptors, and painters interested in iconography and moral representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for representing abstract virtues and vices in visual art and poetry, with attention to symbolism vs personification, attributes, expression, classification, and fidelity to original intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism (as a mode of representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism is 'the setting forth of a great truth by an imperfect and inferior sign' (example: the phoenix for the hope of the resurrection). It is 'almost always employed by men in their most serious moods of faith' and used by those who are true believers in what they symbolize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer symbolism when aiming at solemn, spiritual truths; use imperfect signs that point beyond themselves. Symbolism should be used sparingly and in contexts of sincere faith or deep seriousness rather than mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification (risks and proper use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification is 'the bestowing of a human or living form upon an abstract idea' and is 'in most cases, a mere recreation of the fancy, and is apt to disturb the belief in the reality of the thing personified.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trivial or flippant personifications that undermine the reality of the subject. Personification can be 'thoroughly noble and lovely' when used by early, earnest masters whose imagination does not overthrow faith; aim for spiritual vitality rather than mere fanciful decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing duties with virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The text criticizes 'the confusion of duties with virtues, and the vain endeavor to enumerate the various offices of charity as so many separate virtues' as a point of weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or analyzing iconographic schemes, do not mistake particular charitable acts or duties for distinct virtues; prefer coherent, philosophically-grounded lists of virtues rather than morbidly accurate inventories of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid morbid accuracy of classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'general tendency to a morbid accuracy of classification' (late Renaissance) is presented as a weakness accompanying excessive personification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist over-systematizing or over-enumerating symbolic elements purely for classificatory neatness; such precision often reduces spiritual depth and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the scheme of virtues to the work's religious/viewpoint context
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'number and nature of the virtues differ considerably... according to their own views of religion, or to the manner of life they had in mind to illustrate' (example: Giotto's different lists for Assisi and the Arena Chapel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and arrange virtues so they reflect the theological, institutional, or social context of the work—monastic, civic, chivalric, etc.—rather than imposing a universal list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contraries to clarify meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning 'from contraries' helps interpretation: vices personified opposite virtues reveal 'the particular idea of the contrary virtue in the mind of the writer or painter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design or analyze paired representations (virtue vs vice) so that the antagonist figure elucidates the precise moral content intended for the virtue; contrast is a deliberate interpretive tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of attributes and emblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues should be accompanied by meaningful objects or gestures (examples: Faith with cross/key/scroll; Prudence with book and compasses; Charity with flames/loaves; Hope looking to an outstretched hand in sunbeams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select attributes that concisely communicate the virtue's essence and theological or philosophical associations; prefer historically and iconographically consistent emblems to arbitrary props.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive, spiritual execution over mere literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective personifications (e.g., Dante's burning Charity) convey 'exquisite and spiritual expressions of Christian truth' and surpass literal, domesticized depictions (e.g., Reynolds's nurse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek representations that evoke inner spiritual reality and intensity rather than literal, mundane, or sentimental imagery; stylistic subtlety and spiritual feeling are virtues in depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain forethought/anticipation in Prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence's 'truly distinctive character, namely, forethought,' is often underrepresented; Giotto expresses vigilance but not enough of anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting Prudence, emphasize elements that imply forethought, planning, and anticipation (e.g., Janus-headed imagery, convex mirror, instruments suggesting measurement), not merely caution or vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance should moderate passions, not merely indicate abstinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance is often 'confused with mere abstinence'; properly, it is 'the moderator of all the passions' (Greek sôphrosynê) and may be represented with bridled speech and practical restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict Temperance with symbols suggesting governance of all desires (bridle, sword bound to scabbard), rather than only food/drink abstention; show intellectual or moral control, not only physical restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope as the testing/defining virtue of Christianity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hope is 'the most distinctively Christian' and 'the testing virtue' by which one may determine whether one is truly Christian; its representation should show devotional longing toward heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent Hope with devotional posture and directedness toward divine assistance (e.g., praying hands, gaze toward outstretched divine hand, winged rising), distinguishing it from mere charity or faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity aided by inscriptions when iconography is ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Some figures (e.g., 'Discord') 'need the inscription above to assure us of their meaning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inscriptions or textual labels to disambiguate figures whose attributes or posture alone might confuse viewers, especially in public or polyglot contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve expressive detail in copies and restorations
rubrics_metrics.description: Renaissance copies sometimes 'injure' originals by altering direct and expressive elements (example: replacing showering coins from a hand with a salver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When copying, restoring, or adapting earlier works, preserve the original's expressive gestures and iconographic economy; avoid substitutions that diminish immediacy or alter intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification must retain spiritual vitality to be noble
rubrics_metrics.description: Early personifications are 'more spiritual and vital' and 'thoroughly noble and lovely' when produced by masters whose fancy cannot overthrow faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that personified figures possess internal spiritual coherence—gesture, expression, and composition should reinforce belief in the abstract quality they embody rather than mere decorative inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physical action to communicate moral state
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong personifications employ vividly telling acts (examples: Despair 'thrusting a dagger into her throat, and tearing her long hair' to indicate hopelessness; Fortitude tearing a lion's jaw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey moral intensity through decisive, metaphorically appropriate bodily actions and poses rather than passive or generic stances; the act should symbolically correspond to the inner state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic series should reflect civic or cultural moral emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Different civic traditions emphasize different virtues (Venice's series includes 'Honesty' and 'Alacrity' implying industry; Northern art ranks 'Industry' highly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose virtue-programs that reflect the moral priorities of the patron, city, or culture; do not transplant another context's hierarchy of virtues without adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating saints and virtues in liturgical or devotional lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Later Litanies confuse virtues with saints ('St. Faith, St. Hope, St. Charity, and St. Chastity'), marking a decline in symbolic clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep personified virtues distinct from the cult of individual saints in design and naming; maintain theological and iconographic distinctions so devotional practice does not reduce symbolic meaning.
